title: Making paper clay from an air-dry base
subtitle: Adding paper fibres to air-dry clay to create a crack-resistant body for large or flat work
excerpt: Paper clay is air-dry clay mixed with shredded paper fibres. The fibres bridge cracks as the clay shrinks during drying, allowing larger and thinner pieces than pure air-dry clay can support. Commercial paper clay is available, but making your own from standard air-dry clay gives you control over the fibre content and costs less.
sourceNotes: Paper clay preparation methodology derived from studio ceramics practice where paper pulp addition to clay bodies is documented from the 1990s onward as a technique for reducing cracking in large or thin work.

glossaryTerms.definition: Clay body with paper pulp fibres added, which dramatically reduces cracking during drying and allows large flat work or thin sections impossible in standard clay.
Kneading clay to homogenise texture and eliminate air pockets before building.
Fully air-dried clay with all water evaporated. Paper clay is more robust at bone-dry than standard air-dry clay.

content.text: Standard air-dry clay cracks when it dries in large flat sheets because the outer surface shrinks before the centre, and the clay has no reinforcement to bridge the crack.
Paper clay

solves this by introducing paper fibres that hold the clay matrix together as moisture leaves. The fibres also make paper clay lighter when dry, stronger at thin sections, and joinable even when bone-dry (a bonus for multi-part sculptural work).
Making paper pulp

Tear toilet paper, tissue paper, or newspaper (newspaper adds grey colour: avoid for white clay) into small pieces. Fill a bucket one-third full with water and add the paper. Leave to soak for at least 30 minutes.

Break up the softened paper by squeezing and rubbing it between your hands in the water until no visible sheets remain: only loose fibres in the water. The mixture should look like pale milky water with fine fibres suspended in it.

Squeeze out as much water as possible from the pulp: press it in a cloth or through a sieve: until you have a damp but not dripping pulp mass. The correct moisture level for the pulp is slightly wetter than a well-wrung sponge.
Mixing paper clay

Flatten a block of air-dry clay on a clean work surface and add the paper pulp a small handful at a time. The ratio to aim for is approximately one part pulp to four parts clay by volume: this gives crack-resistance without making the clay too stiff. Higher pulp content (up to 1:2) increases crack-resistance further but makes the clay harder to smooth.
Work the pulp into the clay by folding and pressing repeatedly:
wedging
in the same way as standard clay. The pulp distributes slowly; continue wedging for five to ten minutes until no clumps of visible pulp remain and the clay is a consistent colour throughout.

If the clay becomes too wet from the pulp moisture, spread the mixed clay on an absorbent board and allow it to stiffen for 10 to 15 minutes before continuing. If too stiff, add a few drops of water and work back in.
Working with paper clay

Paper clay handles very similarly to standard air-dry clay for rolling, pressing, and slab building. The surface is slightly textured from the fibres: smooth over with a damp sponge or finger. The main difference is that paper clay tolerates thinner sections and larger flat areas without cracking during drying.
A useful property: paper clay can be joined even at
bone-dry
: apply wet paper clay to a dry paper clay section and the join holds as it dries. This is not possible with standard air-dry clay (bone-dry clay joints break without score-and-slip at leather-hard).
Common mistakes
Visible paper lumps in the finished piece: pulp not broken down sufficiently. The pulp must be reduced to individual loose fibres, not clumps, before mixing.
Clay still cracking despite paper clay: pulp ratio too low, or wall thickness still uneven. Increase the pulp ratio and ensure even thickness throughout.
Finished surface rough and fibrous: too high a pulp ratio, or fibres not fully integrated. Smooth with a damp sponge while the clay is still fresh; sand lightly when bone-dry before painting.

rows.problem: Paper clay goes mouldy in storage
rows.cause: Sealed in airtight bag while still damp; paper fibres encourage mould growth in humid conditions
rows.fix: Use paper clay fresh where possible. If storing, add a small pinch of salt to the clay and seal. Store in the fridge for short periods.

rows.problem: Clay falls apart when dry: crumbles at the edges
rows.cause: Too high a pulp ratio; fibres are dominant and the clay matrix is insufficient to bond them
rows.fix: Reduce pulp to no more than 1:4 by volume. Re-make with lower pulp content.
